speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: TRIBUTES TO HON. LUCIEN LAMOUREUX ON TENURE IN OFFICE AS SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would not want this occasion to pass as I understand that today constitutes a record in terms of your length of service as Speaker in this House of Commons. I do not rise simply because of the length of your service but because I do not believe members of this House would want the occasion to pass without reference to it and an opportunity to pay tribute to you.

Mr. Speaker, I would also like to congratulate you for your services as Speaker of the House, notably for your impartiality and your achievement regarding the maintenance of order and a sense of equity in the House of Commons-

It has been my privilege to serve under you in this House, although for not a long period of time. Indeed, I suffer the disadvantage that you are the only Speaker under whom I have served in the House. But even so, I feel that I can speak with great confidence and with the full support of members on all sides of the House in expressing gratitude to you for the service you have rendered as Speaker. In saying this, of course, I am not suggesting your service is about to terminate or anything of that sort. I simply want on this occasion to pay my humble respects to you and to express my personal gratitude and, I am sure, the gratitude of all members of the House for your impartiality.

maintopic: TRIBUTES TO HON. LUCIEN LAMOUREUX ON TENURE IN OFFICE AS SPEAKER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: TRIBUTES TO HON. LUCIEN LAMOUREUX ON TENURE IN OFFICE AS SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to join, on behalf of all my colleagues, with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) in the greetings that are being extended to Your Honour today. A couple of weeks ago many thousands of people in the United States and Canada were quite excited over the saga of Hank Aaron. They were counting his home runs. The day was reached when he was only one short of Babe Ruth's record, then came the day when he equalled that record, and then the day when he passed it.
When we were meeting on Thursday of last week I was conscious of the fact that we were in the midst of our own saga, that Your Honour was only one day short, and that on Friday you would equal the record of the Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux of being in the chair for eight years, two months and 25 days. Today your record is eight years, two months and 28 days. May I point out, also, that unlike the Hon.
Rodolphe Lemieux, you were also Deputy Speaker for a period of time, which makes a total of ten years and eleven months that you have been in the chair. My hon. friend across the way suggests Your Honour has two more years to go. I do not know why the member stops at two years; I believe when we have a good Speaker we should keep him.

maintopic: TRIBUTES TO HON. LUCIEN LAMOUREUX ON TENURE IN OFFICE AS SPEAKER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: TRIBUTES TO HON. LUCIEN LAMOUREUX ON TENURE IN OFFICE AS SPEAKER
speechtext:
Without giving the House all the statistics that I enjoyed looking up in preparation for this moment, I should like to draw attention to the contrast between the period between 1922 and 1930 when Mr. Speaker Lemieux set the record and the period during which Your Honour has surpassed it. That other period was one of excitement and drama. During those years there was Beauharnois and the Customs scandal. There were minority governments. In fact, although the Liberals were in power most of the time, they never had a majority by themselves. They were kept going by Progressives and Liberal-Progressives. There was also that interesting occasion when the government fell because a member forgot he was paired and voted when he had not intended to do so!
In my view, the most important thing that happened in that period was when Mr. Woodsworth and a few of his colleagues got the first old age pension bill out of a minority government. This demonstrates what a small party can do, and we are still doing it.
The other point I would like to make is that although Mr. Lemieux was in the chair for eight years, two months and 25 days, during that period of time the House was in session only three years, four months and seven days. This is an indication of how times have changed, for while you have been in the chair, during the past eight years and nearly three months, the House has been in session seven years, eight months and four days, and I suspect that no one knows it better than yourself.
In addition to noting these statistics, I join the Leader of the Opposition in a tribute of praise to Your Honour. Unlike the Leader of the Opposition, I could make comparisons. You are the eighth Speaker under whom I have served in this House. There have been some good ones, but in terms of impartiality, fairness and a sense of humour that enables you to carry this House through, so far as I am concerned, and I think I speak for all members of the House, you are tops.

When it comes to statistics, I have them off the record. The hon. member has them on the record before him.
I want to say a word which, at the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition, will add to what he said. We have had many experiences over the years. However, one that I shall always recall, without making any identification, is of a Mr. Speaker who during a frighteningly caustic debate rose in his chair and said, "Order. As long as I sit in this chair there is going to be a minimum of decorum in this House". Today and in recent years we have had a maximum of decorum, and I join those who have spoken of your wisdom, wit and of the fact that above all, regardless of difficulties that necessarily follow in the office that you hold, you have been an ornament to the position of Speaker of the House of Commons.
The speakership is not a dangerous position to hold today. It was originally when those chosen at Westminster had to be dragged to the chair. I never found, in my period of office, that anybody had to be dragged in in order to be honoured as the first commoner of the House of Commons.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRIBUTES TO HON. LUCIEN LAMOUREUX ON TENURE IN OFFICE AS SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is appropriate to the way in which we conduct the affairs of this House that the first tribute should come from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and the last from the spokesman for the government. I hope that the opposition in its tributes has recognized, as I have, the fairness and dignity with which you have conducted the proceedings of the House of Commons. You have treated us all as equals, whether we happen to be in a slight majority or slight minority.
May I say to you, Sir, that it is a singular accomplishment to have been Speaker of the House of Commons for

longer than anyone else. Not only have you served with length of service; you have served as Speaker of this House with a charm, distinction and fairness that no other Speaker has exceeded regardless of the time he occupied the chair. So, Mr. Speaker, we all want you to continue as Speaker as long as you feel able to serve. I share the view of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that when we have a good Speaker, we want to keep him as long as possible. Whether this comes about as a result of delay in election, or for another reason, really does not matter. We should like to have you there for as long as possible.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRIBUTES TO HON. LUCIEN LAMOUREUX ON TENURE IN OFFICE AS SPEAKER
speechtext:
I apologize to hon. members that this subject has taken so much time. I will try to exercise the same discretion that I seek of hon. members when they rise on motions under Standing Order 43.

I would simply like to thank the hon. members who have had the kindness to express such generous feelings about me. I have no delusions, for I know perfectly well that these tributes are not directed to my humble person but to the position that 1 have the honour of occupying as Speaker of this House.

The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) said a moment ago that he had served under a Speaker for a certain number of years. I was rather shocked by that expression. 1 always thought it was the Speaker who served under a House. I have always felt that way and, I might say, at times it has been my impression that sitting under one House or another, or under certain members, has been a rather heavy burden to carry. What has made it easier for the Speaker has been the wonderful co-operation hon. members have extended to him at all times. Obviously, the Speaker is at the mercy of hon. members.
We all believe in the institution of parliament and believe, I am sure, that central to that concept is the speakership. The speakership cannot continue and parliament therefore cannot operate effectively without the support of all hon. members. I have received that support at all times. I am thankful and grateful to hon. members for that generosity, for their tolerance and understanding, and I extend my thanks to them at this time.
I was tempted to rise a few times while hon. members were delivering some very interesting speeches to remind them that long standing tradition prevents hon. members from either criticizing or commending the Chair. I might say that it is easier to apply the first stricture rather than the second. That is why I resisted the temptation and did not interrupt hon. members.

In any case, I thank my hon. colleagues not only for their kind and generous words, indeed too generous, and I pledge as I have done on my first election to the Chair to continue to do my best to serve this House, to serve hon. members and this parliamentary institution in spite of all its intellectual weaknesses, all its human failings which are the lot of each of us, but also most sincerely, with the enthusiasm that hon. members deserve.
April 15, 1974

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEDICAL CARE FOR INDIANS IN PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
1. Canada shares the costs of medical and hospital services provided to residents of Quebec and other provinces, including Indians and other native people. Federal contributions in respect of those costs are made under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act and under the Medical Care Act. The payments are determined as follows: (a) Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act: Quebec has chosen to opt out of this federal program, with the result that the federal contribution to the Quebec Hospital Insurance Program is made through tax abatement calculated by the Department of Finance and not under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. (b) Medical Care Act: In any year that a province participates under the Medical Care Act it receives a contribution based upon the total costs of all participating provinces and territories providing medically required services to Canadian residents. The total federal contribution is equal to 50 per cent of this total cost and is distributed among the provinces in proportion to their insured populations. Approximately 90 per cent of the contribution is made, based on estimates, in equal monthly installments during the fiscal year. The remainder is paid in the following year when the actual audited costs of all the provinces are known.

April 15, 1974

financial markets in recent weeks. I suppose that this world wide increase in interest rates reflects the mounting evidence of the strength of global inflationary forces. subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill has been extensively covered in this House both on second reading and in committee, but I make no apology for speaking on it again today because an event arose today which has to do with the bank rate. I referred to it during the oral question period. This points out in a very clear way the sort of band-aid program the government has in mind, if it has any in mind, to deal with inflation.
Loans Acts Amendments
We have gone from one step to another on a purely ad hoc basis.
The minister now says, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) finally agrees, that inflation and its inflation psychology is the most serious economic problem facing Canada today. The government reminds me of a doctor who, having been asked to correct a bleeding aorta or another major organ in a man's system which causes blood to come to the surface in large amounts, simply applies a band-aid. When the blood comes out further, he puts on another band-aid. He will either run out of body on which to put band-aids or he will run out of band-aids.
Instead of carrying out the deep surgery that is required on the present economic crisis in this country, the government simply throws up its hands and in excuse says, "Look at all the inflation in other countries of the world." Quoting the Wall Street Journal the other day, the Prime Minister boasted that Canada's economy was much better than any other.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext: Have you read the article? You ought to read the whole thing.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
That reminds me-and I have used this simile before-of the chap who said, "My, isn't that a great telephone pole you have sticking in your eye." The reason he has difficulty establishing any relationship between himself and anybody else is that he has two fence-posts in his own eyes, yet the man with the telephone pole is supposedly worse off.
It is no comfort to Canadian businessmen, farmers and fishermen who are supposedly to benefit under the act and these amendments that inflation keeps galloping and galloping. It is almost like a terminal cancer growing without control by the government. The minister cannot assert that he is imposing any controls on the growth of inflation on Canada today: the facts are dead against him on that point.
We will see just what is the effect of this change. I want to relate it particularly to this act. I first want to establish something in the mind of the minister, if I can get his attention for a moment. I want to make this point in deadly seriousness for the minister, his advisers and speechwriters. When a question is asked from this side, as I asked this afternoon, that is not to indicate that it is admitted policy or asserted to be policy from our position. The minister has more than once totally misrepresented questions directed to him by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies), and he may have done the same with some of mine.
I want to say this. If in asking a question we refer to an existing set of facts, or ask the minister to explain government action in light of something else, that does not mean there is inevitably criticism of the first part or necessarily of the second part. We are asking the minister to explain, as I did this afternoon. I want to make that very clear.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
It is not the question. It is the preamble.

April 15, 1974

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
There was no
preamble.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext: I am not talking about this afternoon's question.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
There is no question about other preambles either. We have witnessed a beautiful job of taking things out of context, particularly during the question period when one is attempting to elicit information. However, let us look at this in today's context in relation to the bill before us. The minister and the government have the corporate tax cuts as a measure to stimulate employment in Canada and especially to counteract DISC. That was the primary purpose. Certain tax cuts were advocated and put into place for corporations engaged in manufacturing and processing. That is point number one.
Point number two is that the principal beneficiaries are located in central Canada, primarily in Ontario. It is a fact that qualifying manufacturing industries are concentrated in Ontario. The proportion of economic activity tied to manufacturing and processing is highest in Ontario, and to a somewhat lesser degree in Quebec, certainly along the St. Lawrence region and in the city of Montreal, more than in other regions of Canada. According to the minister's survey, these corporations have benefited considerably from this legislation. We will take that as fact number two.
I then come to fact number three. This is where I want the minister to explain the apparent paradox in government policy. On the other hand we have a fiscal measure which is designed to benefit a limited part of the Canadian economy. It is not even across the board or across the country because the effects are not even in all parts of the country. Even in my province of Alberta, where there is a good deal of manufacturing and a wide corporate structure, much of it is related to the oil industry. The oil and natural gas industries are specifically excluded from the minister's fiscal benefits for corporations; therefore Alberta does not benefit from that tax cut to the same extent as may do other provinces.
Let us look at the impact on small business. Even though it may be engaged in manufacturing and processing, it will be much affected by the new bank rate and the new prime interest rate. Let us look primarily at the kinds of small business in those parts of the country where the proportion of the economy of small business of a nonmanufacturing and non-processing character, plus farming and fishing, will be hit by this move today. There are certain factors which, taken in isolation, would justify an increase in the bank rate. As a theoretical exercise it would be perfectly fine. But what is the result when one looks at the whole picture?
This afternoon I invited the minister to give us the benefit of the government's views as to the effect of its latest monetary measure. What effect is this increase in the bank rate and the consequent increase in the prime rate likely to produce? Will it be to slow down business activity, and where and to what degree? I put it to the minister that it will, and that the people who will be hit first and hardest are those struggling in the more disad-

vantaged areas of Canada. In reply to a question this afternoon, the minister indicated that the effect of DREE, the placing of expansion loans in the less economically advanced areas, would be to smooth out some of the rough edges. But with all due respect to the hon. gentleman, he is feeding us a lot of tripe because DREE does not operate that way. DREE itself requires close examination in respect of its economic impact as well as its political impact. In many areas, the only justification I could find for a number of DREE loans is the political IOU's which will be left.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext: That is cynical.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
I am being practical. One has to judge by results. The minister said something about DREE and the Alberta incentives program. Well, the Alberta program was born out of frustration with this government's oil policy. Another factor was the inflexibility of the corporate income tax structure. The Alberta government has undertaken to establish a corporate tax structure with incentives in order to develop more industry. This was not the result of any positive action by the government opposite. And when we consider the program will not be effective until 1977, I cannot understand how the minister could relate it to the increase in the bank rate just announced, and that is what I was talking about.
The minister spoke about the establishment of a petrochemical industry in Alberta. When cabinet ministers make statements like that, we realize how divorced they are from the situation in Alberta. I dare say that outside the area of Sarnia, Ontario, the constituency represented by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) and the one represented by my hon. friend from Pembina (Mr. Hollands), have as high a concentration of petrochemical plants as any region in Canada, if not higher. And there are more going in. This will lead to the establishment of a petrochemical industry, the minister says. Mr. Speaker, all we can hope from the present government is that it does not act in such a way as to hinder the proper development of the petrochemical industry.
A number of hon. members taking part in this debate have spoken about the inadequacy of the ceilings on these loans. I would point out that the loans are not coming from government funds. For example, loans under the Small Businesses Loans Act are made by the chartered banks and so are loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Now the treasury branch of Alberta has been brought in. If I might be allowed to reminisce for a few moments, it occurs to me that somebody by the name of William Aberhart must be turning in his grave.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext: He must be smiling.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
I remember that in the years between 1935 and 1940 there was no deadlier enemy of William Aberhart than the Canadian banking system. I recall the criminal libel trials about the bankers' toadies. Now the Alberta treasury branch, established under the aegis of the government he then led, has achieved almost the status of a bank. As time goes on, strange things happen. The only reason for this piecemeal recognition of the Alberta treasury branch and other quasi-banks is that the federal government did not have the backbone to
April 15, 1974

insist that all instituttions which carry on a banking function are caught by the legislation dealing with deposit insurance.
The sooner a government at the federal level recognizes that we should deal with banking and credit in this country on the basis of totality, the better. As things are, the chartered banks and a few other institutions are the only institutions qualified to lend under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Yet the chartered banks hold only 37 per cent of the deposits in the country. All the other depositreceiving institutions carry on banking functions to a greater or lesser degree. The government refuses to recognize this fact by introducing appropriate banking legislation to deal with all institutions which engage in the business of banking. There are many shortcomings in the banking system, but that is a subject for another debate.
I come back to the point I was making. I hope the minister will intervene at this stage of the bill and turn his attention to the paradox which has resulted from the monetary action taken by the Bank of Canada and approved by the government as it affects fiscal measures in other areas. Perhaps he can explain this paradox. If he can, so much the better. I am not trying to make him look like a chump who has failed to do his homework.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the bill was being considered on second reading we were debating it, as we were on other occasions when these acts were sought to be amended, on a rather narrow base, namely, the specific application of, say, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act to fishermen or the application of the Farm Improvement Loans Act to farmers, as the case may be. I think it was demanded of us that we do this because of the very nature of the bills presented. It is difficult to get into a far ranging discussion of banking, banking institutions and interest rates and their effect on the economy, but I think the provisions of the bill are sufficiently broad to permit us to ask ourselves what it is we are trying to do.
I got the impression from the answers the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) gave the House today to various questions about the decision of the Bank of Canada to raise the interest rate, the government's policy, and so on, that he was saying he really was not able to deal with the situation, that he was unable to cope, that there was no mechanism by which he could do anything, or very little, to correct the situation. The minister spoke about Eurodollars, other countries seeking to go in for deficit financing as a result of oil prices having gone up, about the way all of these factors throughout the world have injured poor Canada, and that the poor Minister of Finance was helpless in face of these pressures from outside.
On the other hand, I got the impression that the minister was not really interested in trying to do anything about the situation, that he was content to maintain in Canada an arrangement whereby basic decisions concerning fiscal policy are made by the private chartered banks and lending institutions, not by the Bank of Canada even though the Bank of Canada has some authority in law to establish interest rates.
Loans Acts Amendments
I have listened to advice given me at different times, from the time when Donald Fleming was minister of finance in this House, and he and other ministers of finance gave us the same kind of responses we are now getting when we ask questions about banking and interest rates. The theory usually advanced is that the economy is moving at too fast a pace; therefore it needs to have its pace slowed down. The mechanism for slowing it down is to increase interest rates. The Bank of Canada does this by declaring that the pre-discount rate will be at a certain figure. This is a signal to the private chartered banks and other lending institutions, on a kind of rub-off basis, to raise their interest rates on the theory, so we are told, that if it costs more to borrow money, then those who are contemplating borrowing, either for consumer or business expansion purposes, will think twice. These people will say to themselves, "The interest rate has gone up one-half of one per cent and therefore it will cost me too much money to do what I plan to do and I will not borrow money". The theory is that the economy will then slow down a bit instead of moving ahead at an accelerated rate.
It seems to me that the Bank of Canada has engaged in this practice dating from the historic tight money days of the Liberals in 1955 when Walter Harris was minister of finance.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext: That was 1956.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
My colleague from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) tells me that was in 1956. But from reading about and watching events at the federal level before I entered the federal scene myself, any attempts by the Department of Finance, or the minister of finance, or the government, or the Bank of Canada, to slow down the economy by raising interest rates were defeated at every turn by the chartered banks themselves.
This was because, as a companion piece to the Bank of Canada raising the interest rate in order to slow down a heated economy, the chartered banks would embark upon an advertising program to promote the borrowing of money at the higher interest rate, and they succeeded in getting people to do so. So whatever value there was, in the theoretical sense, in slowing down the economy by raising interest rates, it was negated by the very group they were trying to regulate.
Let me give the House a personal example of what I mean. Recently I walked into the Bank of Montreal just across Wellington Street-though you can walk into any branch of the Bank of Montreal and get the same experience-and saw pretty girls running around with big blue buttons on which is written, "Talk to me". Well, Mr. Speaker, I am just like a lot of others; when I see a pretty girl wearing a button with that inscription, all sorts of visions flash through my mind and I want to talk to her. I asked her, "What do you want me to talk to you about?" She replied, "A ski loan. We will lend you the money to buy skis, to buy ski boots or to pay for your ski lodge fees". I told her I did not ski, so she said, "Then we will lend you money for a car, a house, a fur coat, anything at all". The motive was to promote the lending of money and at a higher interest rate, thus defeating the government's attempts to try to slow down the rate of lending.

There has been a steadily increasing per capita debt in this nation that has been escalating at fantastic rates in recent years and at a steadily increasing rate of interest. An increase in the interest rate of one-quarter or one-half of one per cent has deterred no one, and neither will this one per cent increase in face of the promotional and advertising campaigns embarked upon by the banks to defeat the very intention of the Bank of Canada and the government of Canada.
The result of all this-and this is something that seriously affects small businessmen, farmers and fishermen whom we are discussing in this bill-is that a printing mechanism, a mimeographed system of increasing the money supply, is set up.

speechtext: You'd better believe it.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
My hon. friend in the Conservative Party says I had better believe it, and I do believe it. It has been in existence for at least 20 years to my knowledge, and it was something that was not debated at all during the historic period from 1958 to 1962. The latest figures on the increase in the money supply that I have end in September of last year, though the latest figures go to the end of the quarter ending in December of last year. However, the increase in the money supply over the past year has been something between $6 billion and $7 billion.
Common sense tells us that if the printing presses are running off more $20 and $10 bills than can possibly be absorbed by the rate of production, those bills already in existence are going to lose value. The more money in existence, the less the purchasing power of each and every dollar. I am sure hon. members recall a situation that occurred in Hong Kong some years ago where people were depicted walking down the street with a wheelbarrow piled high with money in order to buy a packet of cigarettes. Apparently the same situation existed in Germany when they tried to deal with the question of loss of purchasing power by printing more money. This resulted only in destroying that which they were attempting to correct. This is the situation we have in this country. We simply cannot afford this kind of luxury.
I would refer to the responses of the Minister of Finance to questions asked today. I submit that the question period does not give the fluidity necessary for a full examination of this question because it places the minister, as I have said on other occasions, or any minister in the position of having the last word in respect of any question and, therefore, in the position of being able to say whatever he likes, to not say what he does not want to say, or to fob off a question or in response to a question to make some declaration he wishes to get across. That is what the minister did today. He did not attempt to deal with the very serious situation facing us if we permit this type of fiscal activity to continue. The minister said he was concerned about the money supply and would permit it to increase only to the appropriate level, not too much but just enough, with no indication of how much is too much.
The minister had no idea on this point because it is the banks which decide what the money supply will be. That decision is made on the basis of how much money they can

lend at the stroke of a pen, or push off on people who are willing to borrow. It does not matter what the interest rate is, because the bank does not lose. If the bank has to pay out, in some cases, 8 Vi per cent for term deposits, it gets it back again on the money it lends, plus another 2 per cent or 3 per cent in order to have a profit and to set aside some additional money to lend and increase the fires of inflation even more.
With regard particularly to this bill and the extent it covers the situation we have before us, we do not have anything before us at this time to try to handle the total mess we are in financially. We do not have before us any amendments to the Bank Act for consideration, which might permit us to deal with the major question. We have before us a bill which relates to fishermen, farmers and small businessmen. I do not intend to repeat the speech I made the other day, except to say that it is our responsibility to establish a fixed interest rate if through this bill it is our intention to guarantee loans. The banks and the lending institutions cannot lose in this situation, and we owe it to the people who borrow under this legislation to say to them that they shall be able to do so at a fixed rate of interest.
I think a rate of 6 per cent, while an arbitrary figure, is sufficient. This should be written into the legislation. We should also write into the legislation a provision that a lending institution shall not deny an application for a loan except for good and valid reasons concerning the viability of the person seeking to borrow. It should not be denied on the basis that the interest rate is not high enough and that the lending institution therefore will not earn sufficient profit. Farmers, fishermen and small businessmen particularly are groups which deserve more than any other group in society because they have no leverage. Certainly after the decisions which were made over the weekend, and the discussions in the House today, I am sure there will be support from all corners of the House for the following suggestion. It seems to me we should write into this bill a fixed interest rate and should also write into it a provision that a lending institution cannot deny a loan except on a good and valid business basis.
In order to do this, I think it would be necessary to revert to committee of the whole. The clauses in which I think this could be done are Nos. 2, 7 and 9. If we move forward in this respect, it might be necessary to make companion amendments to other clauses when we reach that stage. In order that we might fix the interest rate to help farmers, fishermen and small businessmen, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett):
That Bill C-14, an act to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to a committee of the whole for the purpose of reconsidering clauses 2, 7 and 9.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, naturally I did not know an amendment would be moved at this stage by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). I find myself in the position of talking about it without having had too much opportunity to find out what it is all about. However, I gather from the remarks of the hon. member that principally he would like to establish a fixed rate of interest. I would be hard pressed to find myself in dis-
April 15, 1974

agreement with that feature of his amendment. My colleagues say, "Go the whole way". All right; we will go along with the amendment in respect of a fixed interest rate.
Mr. Speaker, I have a few points which might lead to improvement of this bill. Principally, the bill sets out four areas in which it would amend existing legislation. First, it would raise the limit of .eligibility for loans under the legislation for firms which write from $500,000 worth of business annually up to $1 million worth of business. Second, it would increase the total amount of money that could be outstanding in the name of any borrower at any one time from $25,000 to $50,000. Third, it would make new businesses eligible to borrow money, which is secured by the government. Fourth, it would provide that business improvement loans include the purchase of land in respect of the establishment of a business.
The hon. member for Skeena spoke about the financial mess we are in. He is right; we are in a financial mess. Questions were asked during the question period about the decision of the Bank of Canada to raise the interest rate. If I might boil down the words of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), the answer was that it seemed advisable to do so. But I believe there is a very good reason the Bank of Canada found it desirable to raise the interest rate. It raised the interest rate in order to restrict borrowing. I think one simple reason the Bank of Canada found it necessary to take this step is that in recent weeks there has been an unparallelled rush on the money supply by borrowers.
Within the last couple of weeks there were loans to one or more chartered bank from the Bank of Canada amounting to $60 million which normally would have been repaid within a few days, but within a few days that loan was increased to $65 million and ultimately to over $70 million. This is because there was pressure on the chartered banks by borrowers because the money supply was drying up.
In the month of March, lending by chartered banks rose by double the amount that was lent in January and February. Obviously, the reason for this, when you get right down to root causes, is inflation. People are borrowing money to pay off their existing obligations, and they are not saving any money. In my view they are very wise not to save any money, because in the situation in which we live today the man who saves is a fool; he is going to be defrauded of his savings if he leaves them in the bank for only six months. The evidence is there. Statistics Canada has issued another of its doleful reports telling us that clothing is up, food is up, transportation is up, and every single commodity that is a necessary requisite of a reasonable standard of living is going up. As one financial writer put it, the prices of those commodities are reaching escape velocity. It is that reason that has caused the money supply to become short. People put relentless pressure on the banks for loans. And now we have the additional monetary check-the increase in the interest rates.
Against that background we are being asked to consider a bill to help small businesses, to help farmers and to help fishermen. I should like to confine myself to the section of the bill which amends the Small Businesses Loans Act. I
Loans Acts Amendments
have several criticisms of the manner in which that act has been administered in the past and will go on being administered in the future unless there is a change in the attitude of the government and of the minister responsible.
When we assess the value of the act we must first of all determine the extent of its availability to people who require loans. I think it is particularly germane to mention here, as did my colleagues a few days ago, the performance of chartered banks in the field. I will take as an example the year 1972, when we find that the Bank of Montreal made a grand total of 433 loans under this act; the Bank of Nova Scotia made 134; the Royal Bank, 952; the Toronto-Dominion Bank, 181; the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, 358; the Canadian National Bank, 741; others, including credit unions and near-banks, 47-for a grand total of 2,846 loans.
This scarcely demonstrates an overeagerness on the part of chartered banks to participate in this program. This House has heard from more than one member about the lack of enthusiasm demonstrated by banks to lend money under the provisions of this act and how they will steer a businessman, if they can, into more expensive avenues of borrowing. Without proof of that, it is hard to make accusations, but on the evidence that we have it would seem to me, and I think to any reasonable person, that banks are less than enthusiastic about low interest loans.
We have seen that in 1972 the total number of loans was 2,846. In 1973 it was scarcely better; there was a grand total of 3,076. Between the years 1961 and 1973, the first 12 years of experience after the act was made law in 1961, the average total amount lent during those years was $24,286,000. In 1973, the grand total was $31.6 million-once again a very tiny increase over such a long period of time and one which reflects the lack of enthusiasm on the part of the financial establishments to take part in any program which lends money to people at less than the prime or top interest rate.
I think there is a demonstrable need here to make the provisions of this act more available to those who need loans, and this government should take two approaches. The first is a public relations approach and the second is an in-house approach, so to speak. I think the Minister of Finance should consult the heads of chartered banks and make very plain to them the desirability of encouraging the establishment of new, medium and small businesses and the encouragement and development of existing businesses. This is more likely to be brought about under the provisions of an act such as this one than it is when these entrepreneurs are forced to borrow at higher interest rates.
The second thing the minister and his department should do is to make certain that every Canadian is aware of the existence of these provisions. I think there is scarcely a member of the House who will not at least go part way with me when I say that whatever utopian philosophy each of us may espouse for our children and our grandchildren for the year 2050 or whatever, we are faced by the inescapable fact that today we live in a society which, for want of a better term, I will call a free enterprise economy. It is propelled by private industry and private business, and most of that propulsion comes not

from big business but from medium and small business which, I will point out for the second time in this debate, employs more than 60 per cent of all the people who work in this country. They work for medium and small businesses which employ 100 or less employees.
I suggest that if this country is to move at all, if the economy is to grow and businesses are to expand and create the jobs necessary, then it is that segment of the economy that needs encouragement more than any other at this stage. We have now some 500,000 people unemployed in this country every year. As we know, many thousands more enter the job market and there are no jobs for them. We have been living with this unhappy situation ever since 1969. The hon. member for Skeena spoke about the famous tight money days of the 1950s. I remind him that the latest and most disastrous of all the dangerous economic games that the government can play was embarked upon, not back in the 1950s but in 1969 when the government chose wilfully to go against the advice of all the economists that it paid to advise it on its so-called war against inflation. It chose to ignore advice that if it followed the course it intended to, not only would inflation not be halted but harmful high unemployment would follow.
Of course, the Economic Council of Canada, which was the source of that information, was right. The government chose to go ahead and do what its own in-house people told it to do and the country was plunged into the situation in which we find ourselves today. I suggest that if we are going to get out of that mess, as the hon. member for Skeena calls it, we Vvill only do so by encouraging the entrepreneurs, who provide employment by means of small business, to expand; and they can only expand if they have a ready source of money.
I suggest to the Minister of Finance that he should make all Canadians aware of the fact that money is available not only for existing businesses but for new businesses, because we have to broaden the base. That is a very comprehensive provision in this bill. For the first time, a new business can get off the ground in part by borrowing money guaranteed by the federal government. But that is only if businesses know it is available, and a great many do not know that the present act is there. The responsibility for remedying that lack lies with the Department of Finance. I urge a full-scale public relations campaign to make sure that everybody in this country knows about the act. Every Canadian corresponds with his government at one time or another, and certainly the government is in communication with every manufacturer in this country with relation to income tax, health and welfare schemes and the like. There is no reason why in one of these many mailings full and complete information on this act should not be included.
The segment of the economy which is called medium and small business is important enough now, employing as it does nearly two-thirds of the work force, that it should not have to depend on the good graces of half a dozen different departments and 18 separate laws or programs to deal with its federal government. There are many programs beside this one of which medium and small business could avail itself, but they are not under the one

umbrella. I would suggest to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), if he thought the country's business was important enough to be here instead of flying off down south-

speechtext:
It is nothing of the kind. If it were a cheap shot, it would be only fair play. It is long past the time this segment of the economy ought to have had its own department, its own minister and all these programs under one umbrella.
Mr. Speaker, I think the limit of $50,000 on loans is too low. If I were moving an amendment I would suggest to the minister that the limit be raised to at least $100,000. There is no reason why it should not be. Again, it is the monster of inflation. To a firm that does perhaps three-quarters of a million dollars' worth of business in the course of a year, $50,000 is, to paraphrase a former minister of the Liberal government, nothing more than a drop in the bucket when inflation is making everything ruinously costly. To new businesses and those who wish to expand, $50,000 is not a very significant amount of money.
The cost of industrial land is rising steadily. This act provides, for the first time, that land may be included under the heading of a business improvement loan. Industrial land in metropolitan Toronto now costs almost $100,000 an acre. The time is rapidly approaching when rental accommodation will cost as much as $2 per square foot, according to real estate agents in that city. When you figure rental you have to take the land component as one-third of the cost and that will be up by 50 per cent by the middle of this summer. With land going for $100,000 per acre, I suggest the top limit of $50,000 on this type of loan is not high enough.
The pressure is on for all kinds of money from different sources. Statistics Canada reported a little while ago that a survey of selected lending institutions in this country showed that they had on their books $13.8 billion outstanding to Canadian borrowers at the end of February. Chartered banks general loans went up $370 million in one week alone, the week ending April 3, to a total outstanding on their books of $31.01 billion. In a market like that, I suggest there is an even more palpable need for the medium and small businessman to have a readily available source of money, with a reasonable limit, at a reasonable rate of interest.
The minister said the other day that the volume under this act of the money loaned and the number of loans was increasing steadily and that this showed the good faith of the government and of the banks. The evidence is not, on its face, apparent to me. In 1961, the year in which the act came into effect, there were 2,977 loans, and in 1973 there were 3,076 loans. That is an increase of 99 loans over 13 years. That is really not much of an increase in volume, particularly in an economy which we are told, every time we dare talk about inflation on this side of the House, is booming. I do not believe that is evidence that anybody is terribly enthusiastic about this program or that the government has been pushing it. If anybody bears the responsibility for making this program not only available but known, it is the government which sponsors it.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I do not have any difficulty in supporting the principles of the bill, but I am in favour of
April 15, 1974

increasing the limit on borrowing to $100,000 rather than cutting it off at $50,000. As I said, I believe this government should attempt to make those who need the money and would borrow it aware of the fact that it is there. Also,
I think there ought to be a fixed rate of interest. I agree with the hon. member for Skeena on that, and I think it ought to be lower than 8V4 per cent or 8!4 per cent.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, as I said before, I believe the small businessman deserves a better deal. I received partial agreement on this from the minister when, as reported at page 1395 of Hansard for April 11, he said:
I agree that the small businessman has a legitimate grievance in this country. He has seen that big government deals with big labour and big business and he really does not have a segment of the government looking after him.
I just repeat the minister's remarks to him and suggest that the government buttress as strongly as they can the need for a special department to encourage the establishment of new, medium and small industry and to help existing businesses expand, thus helping to create the vast number of jobs that are needed if this country is ever to get out of what the hon. member for Skeena calls, picturesquely but accurately, this financial mess.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I simply wanted to reply to some of the "cheap shot" comments coming from across the way.
The legislation which is now at third reading stage really tidies up three existing acts, the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. Yet it will be a mistake to assume that it is nothing more than tidying-up legislation. Some very useful amendments have been brought in and the legislation has been improved in a very real way. With regard to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), it is my impression, as a freshman member, that the amendment may well be beyond the competence of the House to deal with at this stage. I await with interest the ruling which will be made on the point.
It is clear that some real improvements have been made to the bill now before us. I think we all applaud and approve the increase in the ceiling of loans guaranteed
Loans Acts Amendments
under the three categories dealt with in the bill. Certainly I, coming from the sort of constituency I represent, approve and welcome the proposal to extend farm improvement loans to major repairs and overhauls. That will be significant and important to people who make a contribution by engaging in agriculture in western Alberta. I am sure, as my colleague from Ottawa West (Mr. Reilly) mentioned a few moments ago, that the amendment respecting small businesses under which new businesses will be eligible for loans is a very real improvement. This provision will be of considerable advantage in certain areas of the country like my own where great difficulty heretofore was encountered by people who wanted to launch small businesses.
I think the broader definition of what a small business entails will also be helpful. This is a very much more realistic definition than the one contained in the previous act. Naturally, I welcome the evidence that the minister has been taking the advice of my colleagues from Alberta and has included the treasury branches in the list of institutions which are covered by this legislation.
The point which has been made before, and which can be emphasized, is that the increase in the ceiling from $25,000 to $50,000 is, in effect, an indexing operation given the rate of inflation today. The ceiling has not been doubled, in real terms, under this legislation because our rate of inflation is now reaching the two-figure rate. Because of the lack of interest of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in containing it, it shows every sign of staying that way. It appears we shall have two-figure inflation for some time to come. Instead of doubling the limits on loans which people may need to take out to pay for services, the minister in this legislation in effect has introduced the concept of indexing to enable people to keep up with increased costs they must pay if they are to continue in the fishing operation, the small business or on the farm.
When this legislation has been in effect for some time it will be interesting to review it to see if it is working and if it is helping younger farmers to get into the business of farming. As my colleague, the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton) mentioned the other night, there is a clear need in this country for reform under which we can extend loans and assistance to young people on the basis of character, not simply on the basis of collateral.
I think all of us who come from agricultural areas are aware of the very serious problem posed for the future of agriculture by the fact that the average age of farmers in this country is just over 50 years. I can remember not so long ago sitting in the living-room of a constituent of mine in Green Court, Alberta. In that room were 14 people actively engaged in farming, of whom only one was under the age of 40. That is the kind of situation we face across this country. One reason is, of course, that it is most difficult for young farmers without large collateral, without wealthy fathers standing behind them, to get started in agriculture.
I think one of the faults of legislation such as this has been that there has not been much interest shown in becoming involved in investments which might contain an element of risk. The provincial government of Alberta has been acting much more imaginatively in this field and has
1428

April 15, 1974
Loans Acts Amendments
been prepared to back certain risk ventures in agriculture involving younger farmers as well as others. I think that will be the only way in which we can overcome this situation, because the consistently high and increasing average age of those who would take advantage of this legislation in Canada entails a situation which contains within it the seeds of self-destruction of the agricultural industry. I hope that after this legislation passes into law we shall have an opportunity of seeing if the changes included in it have encouraged younger people to enter agriculture. Personally, I confess to pessimism on this point; I doubt if we will see that kind of change.
I think most of us hope we can soon pass this legislation into law. It is worth noting that we are here today, and that this legislation has a chance of being discussed and passed into law, only because the House decided to sit this week and not to take a holiday. We are doing our best to get this legislation, which will be of benefit to the farmer, the small businessman and the fisherman, through the House. I think, too, that this bill will be passed more quickly than might have been the case because the House showed the good sense to accept the recommendation of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and consider it in committee of the whole rather than in the standing committee which is already burdened with other responsibilities.
I trust, sir, that the amendment introduced by the NDP will not unduly delay the passage of this legislation through the House after adequate debate. I want to make this point: when the minister was replying to questions the other day and to comments from members on this side, he suggested that the amendments-I think I quote his words correctly-are the result of "a major review of the effectiveness of the programs". I have not had the opportunity to look at the agricultural legislation which was introduced today. I think we will have to see, now that that legislation, or some of it, has finally been introduced, whether there is any relationship between that major review and the effectiveness of programs that cater to small businessmen, farmers and fishermen in this country. It is clear, on the basis of evidence before us, that if there is to be any really major review of the effectiveness of these programs, there will need to be a much more comprehensive range of changes than we see in Bill C-14.
I know that the federal business development bank legislation will be before the House before too long. I know the minister suggested in debate the other day that the relationship between the legislation now before us and the legislation to shear away a portion of the present Industrial Development Bank will be very clear when that matter is before us. The minister perpetually lives in hope. I suppose he now expects us to do the same in relation to the effectiveness and thoroughness of any review that is undertaken of the effect upon people who have to live with this legislation, those whose lives and futures are affected by whatever review he has undertaken.
On the basis of the amendments incorporated in Bill C-14, it is evident there is no major, co-ordinated plan to help the farmers, fishermen and small businessmen of Canada. The point was made before that small and medium businesses in Canada account for 60 per cent of

the employment in this country. Despite that fact, they are virtually orphans in terms of policy. As my colleague the hon. member for Ottawa West pointed out a few moments ago, if we are serious about helping small businessmen in particular, we should draw together the various programs, create new programs and bring them together under one heading so that in fact they will have the same degree of attention that this and other governments have given to larger enterprises.
All members who have been active in their constituencies know that one of the most frequent requests is to help some poor businessman sort out the maze of government programs that may be available to him when he seeks to establish or expand. There is no effective help to members of parliament or to small businessmen in this field. At the very least, the government should be considering a program that would pull together in a cohesive fashion all programs that affect small businesses and small businessmen in Canada. It is important to remember that the small operator, the small businessman or woman, is the chief business victim of the current rate of inflation. Corporations have various means of defence; they can pass on the effects of inflation or obtain compensation in other ways. In nine cases out of ten, the small business operator cannot do that.
Small business operators are the victims of excessive government regulation. They spend literally hours each week filling out forms and reports. This makes their lives much more difficult. I draw to the attention of the House that they are hurt in two ways by this requirement. First, they are hurt because it takes time to fill out forms and provide information for the government. Second, they are hurt disproportionately because they cannot afford experts to find the loopholes, the ways around various regulations which affect them, to find out how particular pieces of government legislation might influence or affect their future. They are not simply the victims of inflation, which is evident, but also the victims of a growing and active government. If we have to resign ourselves to this growth in government we must give conscience to the category of business people, the 60 per cent of employers in Canada, who suffer most particularly from the effects of a large and growing state.
I do not have the figures at hand; as a private member I do not have the competence to gather them. However, given the fact that 60 per cent of the employment in Canada comes from smaller operators, it would be interesting to compare the level of government assistance to this group as against the level of government assistance to the 40 per cent employers represented by the large businesses and corporations of this country. Any such assessment to see whether small operators are being prejudiced should take into account the much greater capacity of large and established corporations, particularly the subsidiaries of multinational corporations, to make use of programs and expertise which exist in order to find their way around regulations which might restrain smaller operators, or to find their way through loopholes that inevitably exist in law.
There is one particular matter which concerns me substantially. When the minister spoke the other night he said he was not prepared to take measures insofar as the effect
April 15, 1974

on small businessmen is concerned to ensure that this loan program is working. He made a simply incredible reply to the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain). The hon. member made the point that there is a very real danger of banks refusing to recommend loans under this program to small businessmen, farmers or fishermen who might become borrowers from the bank at higher rates of interest. The minister was full of indignation, but not full of help: he suggested that the obvious recourse for people so affected would be to tell their member of parliament. The minister is nodding his head in agreement. That is the extent of his policy. That is the extent of his commitment to ensure that this program is not abused by bankers across the country. In light of that answer, it is well to ask ourselves what other legislation is monitored so weakly in Canada that ministers wait for complaints to come from individual members of parliament to see if the program is working. Not very many.
Most members of parliament do what they can to keep in touch with their constituents, particularly those who might have problems with government agencies. Even the hardest working private member of parliament would have a very slight chance of learning of every instance of businessmen encountering this kind of treatment from their banks. For one thing, some businessmen just will not go to their member of parliament, regardless of his party, with information about their private dealings with their banks. This is a very serious weakness in the program that was drawn to the attention of the minister by the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte. The minister did not give a serious reply. I hope he will reconsider simply relying on the chance that members of parliament will have these matters brought to their attention so they can transmit them to the minister for some kind of corrective action.
One reason I am particularly concerned about the bill before us is that legislation to effect the capacity of farmers, fishermen and small businessmen to obtain loans has special force on a number of Canadians who reside outside our cities. Of course, there are a number of small business operators, men and women, who make their contribution to the growth of the Canadian economy within the cities of Canada. However, it is obvious that this type of provision for loans to farmers and fishermen principally affects the economic vitality of the smaller communities of Canada. Perhaps it needs restating that when assistance is given to a farmer or fisherman to help mount an effective operation, that assistance in effect helps to generate economic activity in the whole of the region where the individual lives.
While there are small business operations aplenty in the cities of Canada, the fact remains that small business is the only business which comes to our smaller communities. This is in part because of an outdated attitude toward the location of industry, an attitude which is equally at fault whether held by members of the government or senior officials of the public service or when held by large companies.
It is a fact of life that when large or medium sized concerns are considering location options, they settle time after time for the large cities. By and large, it is only small businesses which go to the rural areas. Therefore, legisla-
Loans Acts Amendments
tion of the kind before us is particularly important to Canadians who live outside the major cities. I have spoken in this House on other occasions about my feeling that government legislation is weighted, inadvertently perhaps, against the rural areas-that by placing artificial obstacles in the path it decreases the capacity of those areas to grow.
This government, in particular, appears to believe devoutly in the future which its statistics project, that is, a future in which by far the majority of Canadians will be living in a few of our largest urban centres. The fact that the government believes its own statistics means that unconsciously it follows policies in line with such a prediction. I believe such a future is not inevitable for us, but as long as the government accepts this projection as inevitable rural Canada is in danger. Unconscious discrimination against rural Canada has been evident in a number of the measures brought forward since I first came to this House. For example, the new housing legislation was designed to help larger areas; it did not help smaller areas very much.
The sympathies of the government are evident from the attitude taken toward rail abandonment. They are evident also, in the determination shown by ministers to locate penal and other institutions only in the large centres and to ignore the possibility of extending institutional support facilities to some of the smaller places in Canada. They are evident in such small things as failure to inform rural communities of deadlines and guidelines governing LIP applications, assuming that people who live in these communities can learn about such things by reading the metropolitan newspapers or listening to news broadcasts by metropolitan stations. I do not suggest there is any kind of conspiracy against smaller communities. As I say, it derives from the assumption that the future lies inevitably with the metropolitan areas, while failing to acknowledge any capacity to develop a Canadian identity along different lines by encouraging men and women to start business operations in parts of Canada outside the major centres.
We see evidence of the same approach in the legislation before us. It would be impossible to argue that any particular clause in Bill C-14 is directly prejudicial to rural Canada. Nevertheless, the measure fails to recognize that rural areas rely to a far greater extent than urban areas upon small business enterprises. It fails to recognize that time and time again, in the circumstances of today, small business is the only business which locates in these smaller places, giving them an opportunity to contribute to a balanced Canadian identity and a balanced economy.
The concern which should be foremost in the minister's mind during the few weeks in which he is able to hang on to office should be to devise a system which would encourage people to establish businesses in small communities and invest in small enterprises which, at this point, are the only enterprises ready to set themselves up outside the major cities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to take part only briefly in the proceedings on third reading of Bill C-14. It is not my intention to cover all the points which previous speakers have raised. One of the principal changes in the legislation we are considering

April 15, 1974
Loans Acts Amendments
involves the increase in the limit for guaranteed loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act from $25,000 to $50,000. This is certainly an improvement. It is an umpleasant fact that as a result of inflation over the past few years, not very much can be done with the present maximum of $25,000. Even the proposed new maximum is not very satisfactory under present inflationary conditions. One speaker this afternoon thought the maximum amount should be increased to $100,000 and I would certainly endorse such a suggestion.
One important feature has been omitted from the legislation. It has to do with the fixing of the interest rate. The amendment moved by my hon. friend from Skeena (Mr. Howard) would have the effect of sending the bill back to committee of the whole for further study with a view to incorporating into the legislation a change in that respect. One of the most beneficial moves would be to amend the legislation so as to ensure that these loans would be available at a maximum interest rate of 6 per cent. The cost of borrowed capital is one of the heaviest charges which must be borne by any small business. It seems to me that to fix the maximum interest rate at 6 per cent would be a major factor in helping small business ventures to establish themselves or to upgrade their operations. After all, this is the over-all objective of the legislation.
I know of many small business ventures whose owners have worked year after year for almost no reward, principally because of the burden imposed by a high rate of interest on their capital loans. Many proved unsuccessful, and one of the main reasons was the excessively high interest rate charged on loan capital. The same situation is encountered in the farming and fishing industries. In my view, protection against inflationary interest rates ought to be incorporated in this legislation and I urge the House to take action accordingly. I intend to support the amendment and I trust it will be accepted by the minister. In closing, generally I would say this legislation is an improvement over the legislation now on the statute books. It is my intention to support it, and I hope it will be the will of the House to strengthen it along the lines of the amendment.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACT AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier I had not intended to speak on this bill, but I am prompted to do so in view of the inordinate increase in the re-discount rate announced over the weekend by the Bank of Canada. This change in the bank rate clearly indicates new government policy. It clearly indicates that the government has unveiled its contingency plan to deal with inflation, and the contingency plan is the same plan used with gusto in 1968, 1969 and 1970 in the famous war on inflation. This is the contingency plan which attacks the business community with a meat-axe, increasing interest rates across the board, raising them higher and higher to tighten money supply, without regard for who is hurt.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) was asked today what would likely be the interest rate charged fishermen, small businessmen and farmers, he said it would have to be an interest rate high enough to attract money. Clearly the Minister of Finance has unveiled his contingency plan, the plan we have asked about for over a

year. This contingency plan is Liberal tight money- Turner tight money, if you like. It is the kind of plan we are likely to see when the Minister of Finance produces his budget a month from now or maybe longer. This is why I rise today, Mr. Speaker. The problem that small businessmen, fishermen and farmers face when money gets tight is that they are cut right off because they do not have enough influence with the banks to swing a loan. You can have all the guaranteed plans that you want, but they will not get a loan.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) suggested 6 per cent loans for these people. The minister himself indicated today that interest rates will have to be high enough to attract funds. What does this mean, Mr. Speaker? It means, for the small businessman who is trying to become established, a loan under the terms of the act at 9 per cent, 10 per cent or 11 per cent. When members of the New Democratic Party talk about 6 per cent mortgage loans for housing and for small businessmen, fishermen and farmers, they are talking through their hats, because the government does not care about these people. They will let interest rates rise in order to tighten the money supply, because that is their method of controlling inflation. They tried it before, and with some success. They put a lot of people out of work but the inflation rate was lessened. I suggest this is a pretty serious meat-axe method, but it looks as though this is the contingency plan with which the country is faced.
This bill is, in a sense, an indexing bill. I am going to speak today mainly about the Small Businesses Loans Act. The original act provided for a $25,000 maximum loan for small business: this is being increased 100 per cent, to $50,000. In 1961 a dollar would probably have bought twice as much as today's dollar, so all the government has done is increase the limit of the loan. The existing act fixes gross revenues at $500,000; this bill fixes them at $1 million, double the previous amount. In other words, it is doubling legislation, indexing legislation. The bill is trying to make small businessmen, small fishermen and small farmers think they are getting something when they are not really getting anything at all.
Under the Small Businesses Loans Act there were some 2,800 loans made in 1972 in all of Canada. The minister says with pride that over 3,000 loans were made in 1973 in all of Canada, roughly 600 of which were in the province of Ontario. With the number of branch banks, savings offices and credit unions in Canada today, this amounts to much less than one loan per office. The government has not promoted this legislation at all but has placed it on the shelf. It says it is doing something for small businessmen, farmers and fishermen, but the truth of the matter is it has no intention of doing anything. The government will never tell anybody about the legislation and the government will make sure the banks never tell anybody either.
The fact that only some 2,800 loans were made in 1972 is a pretty good indication that the act has not been used to help small businessmen. No real effort has been made by the government to help small business. The provisions of the act are purely cosmetic. The government will say on the election brochures which it will be issuing in a week or so that it has done something to assist small businessmen, and their speakers will stand on platforms and say
April 15, 1974

what great guys they are. But let the people read today's Hansard and learn there was less than one loan per bank.
